exam_guide_revision: Reviewed v5, 2026-09-26. This is a practical Data Structures & Algorithms track built around developer problems, code, performance, state, transfer, and pattern recognition.

learning_design.unlock_rule: All learning reveals are required. Each node moves quickly through a concrete problem, the obvious failure/waste, the maintained state or invariant that fixes it, the pattern name, a different real-world transfer, and one quick check.
learning_design.mastery_note: The goal is not to enjoy studying algorithms. The goal is to recognize the structure fast enough that an unfamiliar problem starts to look like a problem you have already solved.

glossary.definition: A non-data node used to simplify boundary cases such as insertion or deletion at the logical head.
Last in, first out: the most recently added unresolved item is removed first.
First in, first out: the oldest waiting item is removed first.
A collection ordered by priority rather than arrival order.
The small set of current candidates that can produce the next answer.

authoring_notes: Anti-boring rule set: no optional reveals; no definition-first nodes; no university-course voice; no fake corporate narrative; start with code/data/workload; expose the waste or bug; name the useful state; then name the pattern; finish with transfer.

modules.title: Mutate linked structures without losing data

nodes.title: Linked-list surgery: never cut a pointer before you know what is behind it

reveal.text: You already have `prev` and must remove `victim` from a singly linked chain without losing the rest. You are learning to rewire references while preserving reachability of the unprocessed suffix.

spans.text: You already have `prev` and must remove `victim` from a singly linked chain without losing the rest.
You are learning to rewire references while preserving reachability of the unprocessed suffix

prompts.label: ONE POINTER CHANGE REMOVES THE NODE

annotations.title: Bypass victim
annotations.explanation: The predecessor now points directly to the successor, so the remaining chain stays reachable.

reveal.text: Before every mutation, identify which reference keeps the unprocessed suffix reachable. Takeaway: the links needed to reach both processed and unprocessed parts.

spans.text: the links needed to reach both processed and unprocessed parts

reveal.text: Linked-reference rewiring. Trigger: nodes are connected by explicit references and mutation can disconnect the remaining structure

spans.text: Linked-reference rewiring
nodes are connected by explicit references and mutation can disconnect the remaining structure

reveal.text: Removing, inserting, reversing, and splicing linked nodes are all reachability-preservation problems. Takeaway: pointer updates must preserve access to the remaining chain.

spans.text: pointer updates must preserve access to the remaining chain

reveal.text: To remove victim when prev is known, which link changes? Answer: `prev.next = victim.next`.

spans.text: `prev.next = victim.next`.

glossary.definition: A container holding an item plus one or more references to other nodes.
The node immediately before another node in a linked sequence.

nodes.title: A dummy head turns 'remove the first node' into the normal case

reveal.text: Filter every expired node from a singly linked list, including possibly the real head. You are learning to use a sentinel node to eliminate special-case logic at the list boundary.

spans.text: Filter every expired node from a singly linked list, including possibly the real head.
You are learning to use a sentinel node to eliminate special-case logic at the list boundary

reveal.text: Without a sentinel, removing the first real node needs different code because there is no real predecessor. Takeaway: head mutation breaks the otherwise uniform predecessor-based loop.

spans.text: head mutation breaks the otherwise uniform predecessor-based loop

reveal.text: Create a dummy node whose `next` points to the real head. Now every removable node, including the original head, has a predecessor. Takeaway: a stable predecessor that exists even before the logical head.

spans.text: a stable predecessor that exists even before the logical head

reveal.text: Sentinel / dummy head. Trigger: linked-list operations repeatedly special-case insertion/removal at the head

spans.text: Sentinel / dummy head
linked-list operations repeatedly special-case insertion/removal at the head

reveal.text: Partitioning, deleting all matches, or merging into a new linked result can all use a dummy node to simplify edge handling. Takeaway: invent a harmless boundary node so interior logic works at the edge.

spans.text: invent a harmless boundary node so interior logic works at the edge

reveal.text: After filtering with a dummy head, what should you return? Answer: `dummy.next`, the possibly updated logical head.

spans.text: `dummy.next`, the possibly updated logical head.

nodes.title: Reverse a chain one edge at a time — but save `next` first

reveal.text: You need to reverse a rollback-action chain in place. You are learning to reverse links without losing the unprocessed suffix.

spans.text: You need to reverse a rollback-action chain in place.
You are learning to reverse links without losing the unprocessed suffix

prompts.label: THE ORDER OF THESE THREE LINES MATTERS

reveal.code:
prev = None
cur = head
while cur:
    nxt = cur.next
    cur.next = prev
    prev = cur
    cur = nxt
return prev

annotations.title: Save the rest before cutting
annotations.explanation: After reversing cur.next, the old suffix would otherwise be unreachable.

reveal.text: Think in two regions: reversed prefix and untouched suffix. Save the bridge before you redirect it. Takeaway: previous node + current node + saved next node.

spans.text: previous node + current node + saved next node

reveal.text: Iterative linked-list reversal. Trigger: reverse a single-successor chain in place

spans.text: Iterative linked-list reversal
reverse a single-successor chain in place

reveal.text: The same save-before-mutate discipline appears in tree rotations, graph rewiring, and any pointer-heavy mutation. Takeaway: capture the next reachable state before rewriting the current edge.

spans.text: capture the next reachable state before rewriting the current edge

reveal.text: Which line must happen before `cur.next = prev`? Answer: `nxt = cur.next`.

spans.text: `nxt = cur.next`.

modules.title: Choose LIFO/FIFO from the order policy

nodes.title: When the newest unresolved thing must close first, use a stack

reveal.text: A parser reads nested delimiters or nested transaction scopes. You are learning to recognize LIFO structure from 'most recent unresolved item closes next'.

spans.text: A parser reads nested delimiters or nested transaction scopes.
You are learning to recognize LIFO structure from 'most recent unresolved item closes next'

reveal.text: A queue would match the oldest unresolved opener first, which breaks nested structure. Takeaway: closure order is the reverse of opening order.

spans.text: closure order is the reverse of opening order

reveal.text: Push each opener. On a closer, inspect/pop the most recent unresolved opener. Takeaway: the stack of unresolved nested items in opening order.

spans.text: the stack of unresolved nested items in opening order

reveal.text: Stack / LIFO. Trigger: nested structure, undo, expression evaluation, or nearest unresolved predecessor

spans.text: Stack / LIFO
nested structure, undo, expression evaluation, or nearest unresolved predecessor

reveal.text: Parentheses, editor undo, nested transactions, and DFS call state all rely on last-in-first-out behavior. Takeaway: the latest unresolved item is the next one that matters.

spans.text: the latest unresolved item is the next one that matters

reveal.text: For nested brackets, which opener should `]` try to match first? Answer: The most recently opened unresolved bracket.

spans.text: The most recently opened unresolved bracket.

nodes.title: If arrival order is the policy, do not accidentally build a stack

reveal.text: Background jobs must be handled in the same order they were accepted. You are learning to recognize FIFO state when the oldest waiting item should be processed next.

spans.text: Background jobs must be handled in the same order they were accepted.
You are learning to recognize FIFO state when the oldest waiting item should be processed next

reveal.text: Popping the most recently added job reverses service order and can starve older work. Takeaway: the data structure's removal order contradicts the scheduling policy.

spans.text: the data structure's removal order contradicts the scheduling policy

reveal.text: Enqueue new jobs at the back and dequeue from the front. Takeaway: waiting items ordered by arrival time.

spans.text: waiting items ordered by arrival time

reveal.text: Queue / FIFO. Trigger: first-come-first-served processing or breadth-first frontier expansion

spans.text: Queue / FIFO
first-come-first-served processing or breadth-first frontier expansion

reveal.text: Job scheduling, message buffering, BFS levels, and printer queues all share oldest-first removal. Takeaway: the earliest unresolved arrival is processed next.

spans.text: the earliest unresolved arrival is processed next

reveal.text: If a job arrived first, should a newer job leave the queue before it? Answer: No.

spans.text: No.

nodes.title: Keep only the unresolved candidates that a future value can still matter to

reveal.text: For each latency sample, find the next later sample that is higher. You are learning to avoid rescanning the future by keeping a stack of unresolved positions in monotonic order.

spans.text: For each latency sample, find the next later sample that is higher.
You are learning to avoid rescanning the future by keeping a stack of unresolved positions in monotonic order

reveal.text: For every sample, scanning forward until a higher value appears can become O(n²). Takeaway: many positions repeatedly inspect the same future samples.

spans.text: many positions repeatedly inspect the same future samples

reveal.text: Keep unresolved indices whose answer has not appeared yet. When a new higher value arrives, pop every smaller unresolved sample it resolves. Takeaway: a monotonic stack of unresolved candidates.

spans.text: a monotonic stack of unresolved candidates

reveal.text: Monotonic stack. Trigger: next greater/smaller, previous greater/smaller, or nearest boundary where new items resolve older candidates

spans.text: Monotonic stack
next greater/smaller, previous greater/smaller, or nearest boundary where new items resolve older candidates

reveal.text: Next higher metric, stock-span style questions, histogram boundaries, and warmer-day problems share this unresolved-candidate skeleton. Takeaway: one new value can resolve a suffix of previously unresolved candidates.

spans.text: one new value can resolve a suffix of previously unresolved candidates

reveal.text: When a new value is higher than the stack top, what can you do with that top? Answer: Pop it — the current value is its next higher resolver.

spans.text: Pop it — the current value is its next higher resolver.

modules.title: Keep only the priority frontier you actually need

nodes.title: Need the next most important item repeatedly? Keep only the frontier ordered

reveal.text: A retry scheduler repeatedly needs the job with the earliest next-attempt timestamp. You are learning to recognize when a heap is enough because only the current minimum/maximum matters.

spans.text: A retry scheduler repeatedly needs the job with the earliest next-attempt timestamp.
You are learning to recognize when a heap is enough because only the current minimum/maximum matters

reveal.text: Sorting the entire waiting list after every insertion maintains far more order than the scheduler actually uses. Takeaway: full ordering is recomputed when only one frontier item is requested.

spans.text: full ordering is recomputed when only one frontier item is requested

reveal.text: Maintain a min-heap keyed by next-attempt time. Insertions and removals update only enough structure to preserve the minimum at the top. Takeaway: a partially ordered collection whose root is the next priority item.

spans.text: a partially ordered collection whose root is the next priority item

reveal.text: Priority queue / heap. Trigger: repeated insert + retrieve/remove current min or max

spans.text: Priority queue / heap
repeated insert + retrieve/remove current min or max

reveal.text: Schedulers, timers, merge frontiers, and best-first searches all need the next priority candidate, not a fully sorted array. Takeaway: maintain only enough order to expose the current priority frontier.

spans.text: maintain only enough order to expose the current priority frontier

reveal.text: If you only need the minimum repeatedly, do you need the whole collection globally sorted? Answer: No — a heap maintains enough order to expose the minimum.

spans.text: No — a heap maintains enough order to expose the minimum.

glossary.definition: An interface that repeatedly inserts items and retrieves/removes the item with best priority.
A parent/child ordering rule that keeps the best-priority item at the root.

nodes.title: Top 20 from millions? Keep 20, not millions

reveal.text: From millions of request latencies, keep the 20 slowest values seen so far. You are learning to use a bounded heap so memory and maintenance depend on K rather than n.

spans.text: From millions of request latencies, keep the 20 slowest values seen so far.
You are learning to use a bounded heap so memory and maintenance depend on K rather than n

reveal.text: Sorting all n values costs O(n log n) and stores everything even though the output contains only K items. Takeaway: the algorithm maintains far more candidates than the final answer can contain.

spans.text: the algorithm maintains far more candidates than the final answer can contain

reveal.text: Keep a min-heap of size K containing the current K largest values. The smallest of those K is the only one threatened by a new larger value. Takeaway: only the current best K candidates.

spans.text: only the current best K candidates

reveal.text: Bounded top-K heap. Trigger: streaming/large n + only K extreme items are needed

spans.text: Bounded top-K heap
streaming/large n + only K extreme items are needed

reveal.text: Top slow endpoints, largest files, best scores, and most expensive queries all use the same bounded-candidate idea. Takeaway: discard any item that cannot enter the final top K.

spans.text: discard any item that cannot enter the final top K

reveal.text: For K largest values, why use a min-heap rather than max-heap of all n? Answer: The heap root is the weakest member of the current top K, so it is easy to evict.

spans.text: The heap root is the weakest member of the current top K, so it is easy to evict.

nodes.title: Merge many sorted streams by comparing only their current frontiers

reveal.text: Eight log shards are individually timestamp-sorted. Produce one global timestamp-sorted stream. You are learning to reuse each stream's internal order instead of loading and re-sorting everything.

spans.text: Eight log shards are individually timestamp-sorted. Produce one global timestamp-sorted stream.
You are learning to reuse each stream's internal order instead of loading and re-sorting everything

reveal.text: Concatenating and sorting all records throws away the fact that each shard already did most of the ordering work. Takeaway: existing sorted structure is discarded and rebuilt globally.

spans.text: existing sorted structure is discarded and rebuilt globally

reveal.text: Put the first record from each shard in a min-heap. Emit the earliest, then push only the next record from that same shard. Takeaway: one current frontier item per sorted stream.

spans.text: one current frontier item per sorted stream

reveal.text: K-way merge with a heap. Trigger: merge multiple individually sorted sequences while keeping memory near the number of streams

spans.text: K-way merge with a heap
merge multiple individually sorted sequences while keeping memory near the number of streams

reveal.text: Merging index runs, changelogs, sorted files, or database result streams has the same frontier-only structure. Takeaway: only each sorted stream's current front can possibly be globally next.

spans.text: only each sorted stream's current front can possibly be globally next

reveal.text: After emitting a record from shard 3, which new item do you push? Answer: The next record from shard 3 only.

spans.text: The next record from shard 3 only.
